Hill Shading with R: The Definitive Guide

Level Up Your Maps

Lately, I’ve been revisiting my earlier posts on hillshading and the tidyterra FAQ. I wanted to get a better feel for how to create shaded relief in R and how to combine it with a cartographic color palette. The color and the shading both come from the terrain, but how you put them together changes what you see on the map. My earlier hillshade post · tidyterra FAQ

This post brings together what I learned along the way. I’ll start with the transparency trick I used in my earlier maps, compare it with metR and then build up to the approach I use for the final map.

Data and setup

I’m using an elevation grid for the area around Andalusia in southern Spain. I get the bounding box from mapSpain, download the elevation data with elevatr and project the grid to match the boundary. Every map uses the same grid and tidyterra’s etopo1 elevation palette, so we can see what changes when we adjust the shading or the blend.

library(terra)
## terra 1.9.50
library(mapSpain)
library(elevatr)
## elevatr v0.99.0 NOTE: Version 0.99.0 of 'elevatr' uses 'sf' and 'terra'.  Use 
## of the 'sp', 'raster', and underlying 'rgdal' packages by 'elevatr' is being 
## deprecated; however, get_elev_raster continues to return a RasterLayer.  This 
## will be dropped in future versions, so please plan accordingly.
library(metR)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyterra)
## 
## Adjuntando el paquete: 'tidyterra'
## The following object is masked from 'package:stats':
## 
##     filter
library(ggblend)


# The data
andalusia <- esp_get_ccaa("Andalucia", epsg = 3857)
dem <- get_elev_raster(
  andalusia,
  # z = 7, TODO: Use this in the final plot
  z = 5,
  clip = "bbox",
  tmp_dir = tools::R_user_dir("elvatr", "cache")
) |>
  rast()
## Mosaicing & Projecting
## Clipping DEM to bbox
## Note: Elevation units are in meters.
dem <- project(dem, pull_crs(andalusia))
names(dem) <- "elevation"

Hillshade with a transparent color overlay

I started with the example in the terra help. It calculates slope and aspect from the elevation grid, creates a hillshade with a single light direction and draws a semitransparent elevation layer on top. I used the same idea in ggplot2, with a fixed alpha on the layer that carries the elevation colors. Examples in the terra::shade() help

I use a sun elevation of 40° and light from the west (270°). I first draw the hillshade in grayscale, then extract the plotted colors with layer_data(). That lets me pass the grayscale colors directly to the hillshade layer and use the fill scale for the elevation palette.

slope_1 <- terrain(dem, "slope", unit = "radians")
aspect_1 <- terrain(dem, "aspect", unit = "radians")

# Single shadow
hill_1 <- shade(slope_1, aspect_1, 40, direction = 270)

pal_greys <- hcl.colors(1000, "Grays")

gghill_1 <- ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data = hill_1, maxcell = Inf) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colors = pal_greys, na.value = NA)

# Show

gghill_1

# Get colors

pal_1 <- layer_data(gghill_1) |> dplyr::pull(fill)

plot_brks <- sort(c(0, seq(-2500, 3500, 1000))) |> unique()
ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data = hill_1, fill = pal_1, maxcell = Inf) +
  geom_spatraster(data = dem, maxcell = Inf) +
  scale_fill_hypso_tint_c(
    "etopo1",
    alpha = 0.4,
    breaks = plot_brks,
    labels = scales::label_comma()
  ) +
  guides(
    alpha = "none",
    fill = guide_legend(
      title = "   m.",
      direction = "horizontal",
      nrow = 1,
      keywidth = 1.75,
      keyheight = 0.5,
      label.position = "bottom",
      title.position = "right",
      override.aes = list(alpha = 1)
    )
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect("grey97", colour = NA),
    plot.margin = margin(20, 20, 20, 20),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.key = element_rect("grey50"),
    legend.spacing.x = unit(0, "pt")
  ) +
  labs(x = "", y = "")

Shaded relief with metR

The tidyterra FAQ has a straightforward example using metR::geom_relief(). It draws the shaded relief first and then adds the colored elevation raster. In that example, the opacity of the colors varies with elevation, so more of the shaded relief shows through at higher elevations. tidyterra and metR

ggplot(dem, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_relief(aes(z = elevation)) +
  geom_spatraster(
    data = dem,
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    aes(alpha = after_stat(value)),
    maxcell = Inf
  ) +
  scale_alpha(range = c(1, 0.25)) +
  scale_fill_hypso_tint_c(
    "etopo1",
    alpha = 0.4,
    breaks = plot_brks,
    labels = scales::label_comma()
  ) +
  guides(
    alpha = "none",
    fill = guide_legend(
      title = "   m.",
      direction = "horizontal",
      nrow = 1,
      keywidth = 1.75,
      keyheight = 0.5,
      label.position = "bottom",
      title.position = "right",
      override.aes = list(alpha = 1)
    )
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect("grey97", colour = NA),
    plot.margin = margin(20, 20, 20, 20),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.key = element_rect("grey50"),
    legend.spacing.x = unit(0, "pt")
  ) +
  labs(x = "", y = "")

When I put the two maps side by side, I much preferred the one I made with metR. That sent me back to my original map. Could I improve it by changing the way I combined the hillshade and the elevation colors?

Introducing ggblend

Barney Harris had already tried something along those lines. He used the original version of my Romania map to illustrate how lowering the opacity of the elevation layer can wash out the colors. In his example, he used the multiply mode in ggblend to combine the elevation colors with the hillshade. My ggplot2 blending adventure

Here I’ll go back to the single-direction hillshade from the first map and switch to ggblend::blend("multiply"). Keeping the shading and palette the same makes it easier to see what the change in blending does to the colors.

ggplot() +
  list(
    geom_spatraster(data = hill_1, fill = pal_1, maxcell = Inf),
    geom_spatraster(data = dem, maxcell = Inf),
    scale_fill_hypso_tint_c(
      "etopo1",
      breaks = plot_brks,
      labels = scales::label_comma()
    )
  ) |>
  blend("multiply") +
  guides(
    alpha = "none",
    fill = guide_legend(
      title = "   m.",
      direction = "horizontal",
      nrow = 1,
      keywidth = 1.75,
      keyheight = 0.5,
      label.position = "bottom",
      title.position = "right",
      override.aes = list(alpha = 1)
    )
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect("grey97", colour = NA),
    plot.margin = margin(20, 20, 20, 20),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.key = element_rect("grey50"),
    legend.spacing.x = unit(0, "pt")
  ) +
  labs(x = "", y = "")

Enhancing the hillshading

For the next step, I took the idea of multidirectional shadows from Dominic Royé’s post. He holds the sun’s elevation angle fixed, calculates a hillshade for each of four light directions and sums the results. I’ll keep the multiply blend from the previous map and change the lighting to see how the combined hillshade affects the relief. Hillshade effects

In this map I keep the sun elevation at 40° and average the hillshades from 225°, 270°, 315° and 360°.

hill_2 <- shade(slope_1, aspect_1, 40, direction = c(225, 270, 315, 360)) |>
  mean()

gghill_2 <- ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data = hill_2, maxcell = Inf) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colors = pal_greys, na.value = NA)

# Show
gghill_2

# Get colors
pal_2 <- layer_data(gghill_2) |> dplyr::pull(fill)
ggplot() +
  list(
    geom_spatraster(data = hill_2, fill = pal_2, maxcell = Inf),
    geom_spatraster(data = dem, maxcell = Inf),
    scale_fill_hypso_tint_c(
      "etopo1",
      breaks = plot_brks,
      labels = scales::label_comma()
    )
  ) |>
  blend("multiply") +
  guides(
    alpha = "none",
    fill = guide_legend(
      title = "   m.",
      direction = "horizontal",
      nrow = 1,
      keywidth = 1.75,
      keyheight = 0.5,
      label.position = "bottom",
      title.position = "right",
      override.aes = list(alpha = 1)
    )
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect("grey97", colour = NA),
    plot.margin = margin(20, 20, 20, 20),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.key = element_rect("grey50"),
    legend.spacing.x = unit(0, "pt")
  ) +
  labs(x = "", y = "")

The final map: Stretching the hillshade

I kept coming back to that metR comparison. In an earlier experiment with Swiss elevation data, I compared the shade values behind geom_relief() with the values from terra::shade() to understand why they differed. That experiment gave me the idea of stretching the range of the hillshade before blending it with the elevation colors.

I use the 5th and 95th percentiles of the multidirectional hillshade as the endpoints of the stretch. Values between them are rescaled to the 0–1 range, and values outside that range are clipped to the nearest endpoint.

# Stretching
q <- as.numeric(quantile(values(hill_2), c(0.05, 0.95), na.rm = TRUE))

hill_3 <- clamp((hill_2 - q[1]) / diff(q), 0, 1)

gghill_3 <- ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data = hill_3, maxcell = Inf) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    high = "white",
    mid = "gray80",
    low = "gray20",
    na.value = "transparent"
  )

# Show
gghill_3

# Get colors
pal_3 <- layer_data(gghill_3) |> dplyr::pull(fill)

For the final map I also change the grayscale ramp, using gray20, gray80 and white to get closer to the look of the metR example. The elevation palette and multiply blend carry over from the previous map.

ggplot() +
  list(
    geom_spatraster(data = hill_3, fill = pal_3, maxcell = Inf),
    geom_spatraster(data = dem, maxcell = Inf),
    scale_fill_hypso_tint_c(
      "etopo1",
      breaks = plot_brks,
      labels = scales::label_comma()
    )
  ) |>
  blend("multiply") +
  guides(
    alpha = "none",
    fill = guide_legend(
      title = "   m.",
      direction = "horizontal",
      nrow = 1,
      keywidth = 1.75,
      keyheight = 0.5,
      label.position = "bottom",
      title.position = "right",
      override.aes = list(alpha = 1)
    )
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect("grey97", colour = NA),
    plot.margin = margin(20, 20, 20, 20),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.key = element_rect("grey50"),
    legend.spacing.x = unit(0, "pt")
  ) +
  labs(x = "", y = "")
